claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy's limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness are caused by dislocation pile-ups near internal lamellar boundaries.
An aging treatment can induce coherent nanoscale precipitates at or near the internal lamellar interfaces.
A single-step aging treatment can be optimized to nucleate and grow the proposed precipitates.
The coherent nanoscale precipitates will pin or otherwise impede dislocations.
The precipitates will facilitate more homogeneous plastic flow.
The coherent precipitates can shear under applied stress.
The precipitates will reduce dislocation pile-ups and the associated local stress concentrations.
More uniform strain distribution will delay microcrack initiation and growth.
The precipitates will provide additional strength through precipitation hardening.
The treatment will markedly improve room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or modestly increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing at approximately 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ is an applicable evaluation condition.
TEM and EBSD are applicable methods for characterizing the treated microstructure and deformation structures.
The intervention is applicable to similar eutectic high-entropy alloy systems.
Differences in alloy composition may alter precipitate coherence and effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies a controlled aging heat treatment as the single intervention, whereas the intervention field allows either a single-step aging treatment or a thermo-mechanical process, leaving the intervention non-unique.
